title: Episode 206: The Persian Empire: Cyrus the Great, the Cyrus Cylinder, and the Return of the Exiles
description:
From the rugged mountains of modern Iran arose Cyrus the Great, founding the largest empire the ancient world had ever seen. Unlike the brutal Assyrians and Babylonians who ruled by terror and deportation, Cyrus pioneered a revolutionary imperial philosophy of cultural tolerance, religious freedom, and local self-governance. In 538 BC, Cyrus issued his historic Edict of Restoration—inscribed on the famous clay Cyrus Cylinder unearthed in Babylon—allowing displaced peoples to return to their native lands and rebuild their desecrated temples. Releasing forty-two thousand Jewish exiles under Prince Zerubbabel and High Priest Jeshua, Cyrus restored the sacred temple vessels and financed the reconstruction of the Second Temple in Jerusalem. Under Darius the Great, Persia constructed the Royal Road, the monumental capital of Persepolis, and an elite ten-thousand-man infantry corps known as the Immortals. Discover the enlightened empire that ended the Babylonian exile and rebuilt Zion.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we enter the silver realm of the Medo-Persian Empire. Emerging from the Zagros Mountains, Cyrus the Great transformed world governance, instituting what many historians revere as the first charter of human rights. Here is George with the story of Cyrus the Great, the Cyrus Cylinder, and the return to Jerusalem.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE RISE OF ANSHAN AND THE MEDIAN UPRISING
In the sixth century before Christ, the Persian tribes were small, pastoral vassals living in the rugged highlands of Anshan in southwestern Iran, subjugated by their northern kinsmen, the Medes. But in 559 BC, an extraordinary young prince named Cyrus II ascended the Persian throne. Combining brilliant military tactics with unmatched personal magnetism, Cyrus united the disparate Persian clans. When the Median King Astyages marched to crush the upstart prince, Cyrus rallied his horsemen. In a stunning reversal, the Median army, alienated by Astyages's cruelty, mutinied and surrendered to Cyrus. Rather than sacking the Median capital of Ecbatana, Cyrus treated Astyages with honor, integrating Median generals into his high command and forging a dual Medo-Persian superpower. Cyrus then marched west into Asia Minor, defeating the fabulously wealthy King Croesus of Lydia at Sardis, subduing the Greek coastal cities of Ionia, and extending Persian dominion to the Aegean Sea. By 539 BC, Cyrus turned his gaze toward Babylon, conquering the Mesopotamian empire with astonishing swiftness and positioning Persia as the undisputed colossus of the ancient Near East. Cyrus's early campaigns established a new standard of military chivalry in antiquity. Unlike the Assyrian kings who mutilated and flayed conquered monarchs, Cyrus spared King Croesus of Lydia, appointing him as a senior counselor and preserving the cultural heritage of Sardis. Cyrus's tomb at Pasargadae, a simple stepped limestone chamber inscribed with his modest epitaph, stood as a monument of personal restraint admired even by Alexander the Great two centuries later.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CYRUS CYLINDER: THE CHARTER OF FREEDOM
When Cyrus entered Babylon in October 539 BC, the world expected the typical orgy of slaughter, looting, and enslavement perfected by Assyria and Babylon. Instead, Cyrus astonished the ancient world by enacting a revolutionary policy of imperial benevolence. In 1879, British Museum archaeologists excavating Babylon discovered a nine-inch baked clay barrel covered in Akkadian cuneiform: the famous Cyrus Cylinder. On this historic artifact, Cyrus declared his imperial philosophy: 'When I entered Babylon as a friend and established the seat of government in the palace of the ruler amongst jubilation and rejoicing... my numerous troops strolled through Babylon in peace. I did not allow anyone to terrorize the land... I sought the welfare of the city of Babylon and all its sacred centers... I collected all their previous inhabitants and returned them to their habitations.' Reversing two centuries of Mesopotamian state terror, Cyrus permitted conquered nations to practice their ancestral religions, speak their native tongues, and rebuild their shattered shrines, creating an enduring model of decentralized federal empire that secured loyalty through gratitude rather than fear. The Cyrus Cylinder, often called the world's first declaration of human rights, was buried in the foundations of the Esagila temple in Babylon. Its cuneiform text reveals an enlightened imperial strategy: fostering domestic peace and religious liberty across conquered territories to ensure lasting imperial stability. In 1971, the United Nations celebrated the artifact as a timeless symbol of cultural and religious freedom.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE EDICT OF RESTORATION: 538 BC
For the Jewish exiles living along the canals of Babylon, Cyrus's policy was nothing short of miraculous divine deliverance, fulfilling the exact prophecies uttered by Isaiah more than a century earlier, which had called Cyrus by name: 'He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built; and to the temple, Thy foundation shall be laid.' In 538 BC, the first year of his reign over Babylon, Cyrus issued a formal royal decree recorded in the biblical Book of Ezra: 'Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The Lord God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and He hath charged me to build Him an house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all His people? His God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem... and build the house of the Lord.' Cyrus did not merely permit the Jews to return; he dipped into the royal treasury to finance their travel, and ordered the return of five thousand four hundred gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had plundered from Solomon's Temple. The royal proclamation of Cyrus sent shockwaves of joy through the Jewish communities of Mesopotamia. For the first time in ancient history, an imperial ruler actively funded the restoration of a conquered people's sacred temple from the royal treasury, granting the Jewish elders full authority to draw timber from imperial forests in Lebanon.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE FIRST WAVE: ZERUBBABEL AND THE BROKEN ALTAR
In the spring of 537 BC, a courageous pioneer caravan of forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty Jewish men, women, and children, accompanied by seven thousand servants, began the arduous four-month trek across eight hundred miles of scorched desert back to the ruins of Judah. Led by Prince Zerubbabel, a descendant of the royal line of David, and Jeshua the High Priest, the returnees arrived to a scene of utter desolation: Jerusalem was a ghost town of charred stones, wild thornbushes, and collapsed towers. Undeterred, their first act was to clear the debris atop Mount Moriah and re-erect the altar of burnt offerings, offering morning and evening sacrifices under the open autumn sky during the Feast of Tabernacles. In the second year of their return, with cedar timbers imported from Lebanon, masons laid the foundation stones of the Second Temple. The priests blew silver trumpets and cymbals, singing psalms of praise. Yet the biblical record notes a poignant contrast: while the young shouted for joy, the old men who had seen the towering glory of Solomon's Temple wept with loud voices, seeing the humble scale of the new foundation, their cries mingling in the desert wind. The return journey from Babylon to Jerusalem across the desert was perilous, fraught with heat, thirst, and hostile nomadic raiders. Yet the forty-two thousand pilgrims marched with singing, carrying five thousand sacred vessels of gold and silver back to Mount Moriah, sustained by daily prayers and sacred psalms of ascent.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: DARIUS THE GREAT AND THE IMPERIAL MACHINE
Following the death of Cyrus on the northern frontier fighting nomadic Massagetae horsemen, and the brief reign of his son Cambyses who conquered Egypt, the Persian Empire was reorganized by a brilliant administrative genius: Darius I, known as Darius the Great. Ascending the throne in 522 BC after putting down a dozen rebellions commemorated on the colossal Behistun Rock inscription, Darius divided the vast empire into twenty administrative provinces called 'satrapies,' each governed by a royal satrap, a military commander, and a state secretary who operated as the 'King's Eyes and Ears.' Darius standardized taxation, introduced the gold 'daric' coin that became the universal currency of Mediterranean commerce, and created an elite ten-thousand-man infantry bodyguard called the 'Immortals'—so named because whenever a soldier fell in battle, another immediately stepped into his place, keeping the unit perpetually invincible. Under Darius, the Persian Empire spanned two million square miles, from the Indus River in India to the plains of Thrace in southeastern Europe. Darius the Great's administrative reorganization turned Persia into the most efficiently governed empire of antiquity. His standard gold daric coins and silver sigloi established a predictable economic foundation that fueled international commerce from India to the Aegean Sea, while royal auditors managed taxation records in Susa.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE ROYAL ROAD AND PERSEPOLIS
To bind this colossal empire together, Darius engineered the ancient world's greatest infrastructure marvel: the Royal Road. Stretching sixteen hundred and seventy-seven miles from the Aegean port of Sardis through the heart of Anatolia, crossing the Euphrates and Tigris to the imperial capital at Susa, the highway was paved and guarded by one hundred and eleven post stations. Mounted royal couriers on fresh horses relayed imperial dispatches across the entire length of the road in just seven days—a journey that took three months on foot. Greek historian Herodotus famously marveled at their unyielding speed: 'Neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stays these couriers from the swift completion of their appointed rounds'—words immortalized today on the facade of New York City's central post office. In the Persian homeland, Darius founded Persepolis, the ceremonial capital built upon a massive stone terrace, adorned with the breathtaking Apadana palace hall supported by seventy-foot fluted columns and carved with intricate stone reliefs depicting delegations from twenty-three nations bearing gifts in peaceful harmony. The Royal Road was celebrated by Greek travelers as an unprecedented civil marvel. With fresh horses waiting at every station, imperial couriers carried royal decrees across rugged mountain ranges and deserts in seven days, binding distant provinces to the court at Susa with remarkable speed and security.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SECOND TEMPLE COMPLETED: 516 BC
Back in Jerusalem, temple construction had stalled for sixteen years due to hostile opposition from neighboring Samaritans who bribed Persian court officials to issue halt orders. But under the impassioned preaching of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, Zerubbabel resumed construction. When the Persian governor of the Trans-Euphrates region, Tattenai, challenged their authority, the elders appealed to the original edict of Cyrus. Darius the Great ordered a search of the royal archives: in the fortress of Ecbatana, the original parchment roll of Cyrus was discovered. Darius issued a stern royal decree: not only was Tattenai ordered not to hinder the work, but he was commanded to provide royal tax revenues to pay for construction, warning that anyone who altered the decree would have a beam pulled from his house and be impaled upon it. In 516 BC—exactly seventy years after Solomon's Temple had been burned—the Second Temple of Jerusalem was completed and joyfully dedicated, standing as an enduring testament to the enlightened decree of Cyrus and the unyielding resilience of faith. The completion of the Second Temple in 516 BC marked the exact fulfillment of Jeremiah's seventy-year prophecy. Though modest compared to Solomon's golden grandeur, the Second Temple stood as an enduring monument to divine faithfulness, dedicated with joyous Passover celebrations under Persian imperial protection.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Under the tolerant banner of Persia, the Second Temple rose in Jerusalem, anchoring Jewish identity for centuries to come. But within the marble halls of the royal winter palace at Susa, a mortal peril was gathering that threatened the total extinction of the Jewish people. Next week, we continue our Persian saga with Episode 207: Queen Esther, Xerxes, and the Deliverance of Purim: the palace beauty pageant, the arrogant pride of Haman, Mordecai's defiant stand, the queen who risked death to approach the golden scepter, and the feast of Purim. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
